chapterName: Late Republic: Caesar's Civil War and the Ides of March (49-44 BCE)

questions.question: From which port did Pompey sail to raise an army in the east?
questions.explanation: Pompey left from Brundisium on the heel of Italy. Caesar arrived on 9 March, too late to stop him.
questions.sourceQuote: Pompey sailed from Brundisium, a port on the heel of Italy, to raise an army in the east.

questions.question: Who led the rebellion in Spain that ended at Munda in 45 BC?
questions.explanation: Pompey's sons raised the rebellion in Spain. At Munda Caesar's men wavered and he rushed to the front himself.
questions.sourceQuote: Then came rebellion in Spain, led by the sons of his dead rival Pompey.

questions.question: What compromise did Mark Antony broker after the assassination?
options: Caesar declared a tyrant, his acts annulled
Brutus made consul in Caesar's place
questions.explanation: The assassins escaped punishment, but Caesar's appointments stood. Meanwhile citizens hid indoors and angry crowds later burned the hall where he died.
questions.sourceQuote: Mark Antony, Caesar's fellow consul, brokered a compromise: the assassins would go unpunished, but Caesar's appointments would stand.

questions.question: Why was it striking that 72 lictors marched before Caesar at his triumphs?
options: It was three times a dictator's usual number
It equalled one for each of his victories
It matched the number of senators he pardoned
It was the number granted to Pompey
It was the number reserved for kings
questions.explanation: The lictors carried the fasces, symbols of the power to punish, and 72 was triple a dictator's normal escort.
questions.sourceQuote: That was three times a dictator's usual number.

questions.question: Where did Caesar defeat Pompey's commanders in June 49 BC?
questions.explanation: Caesar won at Ilerda in north-east Spain, and the whole peninsula soon fell to him.
questions.sourceQuote: In June he defeated Pompey's commanders at Ilerda, in north-east Spain, and the peninsula soon fell to him.

questions.question: How did Caesar overcome a tribune who vetoed his seizure of the state treasury?
options: He waited for his term to end
He bribed him with silver bars
He had him exiled to Gaul
He had the Senate overrule him
questions.explanation: Caesar threatened the tribune until he gave way, then took some 15,000 gold bars and 30,000 silver bars. He left the episode out of his own account.
questions.sourceQuote: When a tribune vetoed his plan to seize the state treasury, Caesar threatened the man's life until he gave way.

questions.question: What personal link did Brutus, who sought pardon after Pharsalus, have to Caesar?
options: His mother had been Caesar's lover
He was married to Caesar's daughter
questions.explanation: Brutus was a young aristocrat whose mother had been Caesar's lover, and Caesar welcomed him warmly.
questions.sourceQuote: Among those who sought pardon was Brutus, a young aristocrat whose mother had been Caesar's lover.

questions.question: What did Caesar try to do to Pompey's army at Dyrrachium?
options: Attack it at night from the sea
Starve it by burning its fleet
Lure it into a river crossing
questions.explanation: Caesar tried to wall Pompey in at Dyrrachium, but after months of skirmishing Pompey broke out and forced him to retreat into Thessaly.
questions.sourceQuote: At Dyrrachium, a port in modern Albania, he tried to wall in the army of his rival Pompey.

questions.question: What happened to Egypt's boy king after Caesar's reinforcements arrived?
options: He made peace and shared the throne
He was beheaded on Caesar's orders
He was taken to Rome in chains
questions.explanation: Caesar crushed the Egyptians and the king drowned in flight. The king's regent had earlier besieged Caesar in the palace quarter.
questions.sourceQuote: When reinforcements arrived, Caesar crushed the Egyptians, and the king drowned in flight.

questions.question: How did Caesar react when his most uncompromising Senate enemy took his own life at Utica?
options: He regretted losing the chance to pardon him
He ordered the man's family exiled
He punished the doctor who stitched the wound
He celebrated with a public festival
He had the body displayed in Rome
questions.explanation: The man stabbed himself and tore open the doctor's stitches. Caesar, who prized clemency, regretted not being able to pardon him.
questions.sourceQuote: Caesar regretted losing the chance to pardon him.
